title: Whittled hazel clothes peg
subtitle: Green-wood whittling: a split-peg from a hazel rod
excerpt: A traditional split-peg clothes peg whittled from a single hazel rod. Two tines held apart by a carved wedge notch at the crown. No spring, no hardware, just the tension of the split green wood holding the fabric in place as it dries. One of the oldest and simplest green-wood projects.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for split-peg treen; Beeton's Book of Household Management (1861) domestic whittling section.

glossaryTerms.definition: Freshly felled or recently riven wood, still high in moisture content. Carves easily and retains spring after splitting, which is what makes the split-peg peg work.
A short length of split timber; here, a short section of hazel rod.

content.text: A split-peg clothes peg is a length of hazel rod split partway up its length into two springy tines, with a notch carved at the crown of the split to hold the two tines apart at just the right distance. The spring of the green hazel, still moist and alive in the wood fibres, grips the washing line and the fabric between its tines. As the peg dries on the line it sets slightly stiffer; pegs left out over a season harden into a reliable working tool. This is a first-knife project.
. A straight hazel rod from a coppice stool, freshly cut, about 10 mm in diameter at the thin end and 15 mm at the base.
Grip: four-finger grip on the work; thumb-push grip on the knife. Never make a cut whose blade-path can reach a body part.
Cut direction: push cuts (blade away from body) and thumb-pivot cuts are the default. Pull cuts only with the work braced against the chest and the blade-arc unable to reach anything vital.
Sharpening: a dull tool is more dangerous than a sharp one, the dull tool slips. Strop every fifteen minutes of carving, hone weekly, oilstone monthly.
First aid: keep a styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Apply firm pressure, elevate, and dress. A cut that shows fat or won't close with pressure goes to A&E, not a plaster.
Workspace: stable seat, good light, no children or pets within arm-and-blade reach.

, freshly cut, 12 cm long, 10, 15 mm diameter. Cut from a young coppice rod at the thick-end section for maximum peg width. The section should have no side branches and no obvious knots. Willow works as well as hazel and is even springier, the peg will grip more firmly but may be harder to open.
Sloyd knife, the only cutting tool needed.
Anywhere you can sit comfortably with your lap free. This is the simplest whittling project in the category, no bench, no vice, no special setup.
to flatten two opposite sides of the rod along its full length, removing the bark and leaving two flat faces about 1 cm wide. This gives the tines their even thickness after splitting.

At one end (the crown end, the thicker end), cut a shallow V-notch across the width of one flat face. The notch is 4 mm wide at the opening and 3 mm deep. This notch holds the split open at the right width. A
straight across the base of the V prevents the split running past the notch when the peg is opened.

Place the knife tip at the centre of the notch and push the blade straight down through the rod along the pith, splitting it into two tines. The split should travel down the rod about 8 cm, leaving 4 cm unsplit at the crown (the handle/grip section above the notch). If the split tries to run off-centre, twist the rod slightly in the direction needed to steer it back. The stop cut at the base of the notch arrests the split at the right point.
Use push cuts to round the ends of each tine so there are no sharp corners that could catch on fabric. A light chamfer on the inner edges of the tines at the tip prevents snagging.

No oil finish needed, a clothes peg lives outdoors and in use. Dry in the open air for one to two days before using on the washing line. The bark can be left on the unsplit grip section or stripped; stripped pegs dry faster and last longer.
Willow peg: springier than hazel, good for heavier washing.
Garden-stake peg: 20 cm long, thicker rod, for holding garden netting to canes.
Leave pegs on the washing line rather than in a peg bag, they last longer outdoors with airflow than in a closed damp bag. Replace when the tines no longer spring open.

attrs.symptom: The split runs off-centre and makes uneven tines
attrs.cause: The split followed a knot or a branch scar in the wood
attrs.fix: Start from a straighter section of rod with no side-branch scars. If the split is already off-centre, accept it, one thinner tine still functions. Avoid knots when selecting the billet.

attrs.symptom: The tines snap rather than spring open
attrs.cause: The rod was too dry or too thin
attrs.fix: Use freshly cut rod. A rod under 8 mm diameter is too thin for a reliable peg, it will snap rather than split. Use the thicker end of the hazel rod.
